title: Should a failing security scan block the build — how do you choose blocking criteria, remediation SLAs by severity, and an auditable exception process?
shortTitle: Should a failing security scan block the build — how do you choose blocking criteria, remediation SLAs by severity, and an auditable exception process?
topicTitle: Should a failing security scan block the build

s1_definition.profdef: A build-breaking security gate is a policy in the CI/CD pipeline that fails the build when a scanner (SCA, SAST, container, or secrets scan) reports a finding above a defined risk threshold. A mature gate does not block on every finding; it blocks on severity combined with reachability and exploitability, assigns remediation SLAs per severity, and allows a time-boxed, approved, auditable exception (a "risk acceptance") so the pipeline stays both safe and unblocked.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the security scan as the metal detector at the entrance of National Bank of India. If it beeps for a real gun (a critical, exploitable vulnerability), the guard must stop that person — the build fails. But if it beeps for a metal belt buckle (a low-severity issue in code that never runs), you do not shut the whole bank down; you note it, give it a deadline to fix, and let the person through. And if someone genuinely needs to carry a tool, a manager signs a written, dated, expiring permission slip — that is the auditable exception.
s1_definition.oneliner: Block the build on severity plus exploitability, fix the rest against severity-based SLAs, and allow only time-boxed, signed, expiring exceptions.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A build-breaking security gate is a policy in the CI/CD pipeline that fails the build when a scanner (SCA, SAST, container, or secrets scan) reports a finding above a defined risk threshold. A mature gate does not block on every finding; it blocks on severity combined with reachability and exploitability, assigns remediation SLAs per severity, and allows a time-boxed, approved, auditable exception (a "risk acceptance") so the pipeline stays both safe and unblocked.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the security scan as the metal detector at the entrance of National Bank of India. If it beeps for a real gun (a critical, exploitable vulnerability), the guard must stop that person — the build fails. But if it beeps for a metal belt buckle (a low-severity issue in code that never runs), you do not shut the whole bank down; you note it, give it a deadline to fix, and let the person through. And if someone genuinely needs to carry a tool, a manager signs a written, dated, expiring permission slip — that is the auditable exception.

**One line to remember:** Block the build on severity plus exploitability, fix the rest against severity-based SLAs, and allow only time-boxed, signed, expiring exceptions.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach is to fail the build on any vulnerability of HIGH or CRITICAL severity. This sounds safe but it destroys developer trust, because most scanners produce a flood of findings, many of which are in transitive dependencies that your code never actually calls. When every build goes red, engineers learn to ignore the gate or bypass it, which is worse than having no gate at all. So the real engineering decision is: what exactly do you block on?

The strongest blocking criterion combines three signals. First, **severity** — usually the CVSS base score, where 9.0 and above is Critical and 7.0 to 8.9 is High. Second, **reachability** — does your code actually invoke the vulnerable function? Modern SCA tools like Snyk and GitHub's dependency scanning do reachability analysis, so you can block only on vulnerabilities that are actually callable from your code. Third, **exploitability** — is there a known exploit in the wild? The CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalog and the EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability let you prioritize what attackers are actually using. A sensible policy is: block the build on any Critical that is reachable, OR any vulnerability on the KEV list regardless of CVSS, OR any newly introduced High. You do NOT block on pre-existing Lows and Mediums; those become tracked tickets.

Remediation SLAs are deadlines assigned by severity. A typical banking standard is: Critical fixed within 24 to 72 hours, High within 7 to 30 days, Medium within 90 days, Low within 180 days or risk-accepted. The SLA clock starts when the finding is first detected. The key senior-level nuance is that the SLA applies to the whole backlog, not just the build gate — the gate stops NEW critical issues from entering, while the SLA process drives DOWN the existing backlog over time. You measure "mean time to remediate" as a program health metric.

The exception process exists because sometimes you genuinely cannot fix a finding immediately — there is no patch yet, the fix is a breaking major-version upgrade, or the vulnerable path is provably not exploitable in your configuration. A good exception is never a permanent "ignore" flag buried in a config file. It is a formal record that captures who requested it, who approved it (a security owner, not the developer themselves), the business justification, the compensating control, and crucially an expiry date. When the exception expires, the gate fails again, forcing a re-review. This is what makes it auditable: a regulator or auditor can ask "show me every risk you accepted and who signed off" and you can produce the list.

In a `.snyk` policy file or a Dependabot config you express this, but the governance (approver, expiry, justification) should live in a system of record, not just a code comment. The pipeline reads the policy, evaluates findings, and either passes, fails, or passes-with-logged-exception.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the payments team runs a daily pipeline that scans the application's dependencies. Rajesh, a software engineer, pushes a change and the build suddenly goes red with four findings. The team needs a gate that makes the right call automatically.

Problem 1 — A Critical vulnerability is reported in a JSON library, and the scanner confirms the vulnerable parser method is actually called from the payment-request handler. This is a real, reachable, exploitable risk to money movement. This is exactly how a hard block works — the policy must fail the build immediately because a reachable Critical in a payments path is unacceptable.

Problem 2 — A High vulnerability is reported in a logging dependency, but reachability analysis shows the vulnerable code path is never invoked by the application. This is exactly how severity-plus-reachability works — the finding is logged and ticketed with a 30-day SLA, but it does not stop the release, because blocking here would train engineers to ignore the gate.

Problem 3 — A Critical is reported in a library with no available patch, but the team has a compensating control (the input is sanitized upstream) and a security lead has signed a time-boxed risk acceptance. This is exactly how the auditable exception works — the gate honors the signed exception until its expiry date and then re-blocks automatically.

Problem 4 — A finding appears on the CISA KEV list even though its CVSS is only Medium. This is exactly how exploitability overrides raw severity — attackers are actively using it, so the policy escalates it to a block regardless of the base score.

The code will model a `Finding` (severity, reachable, onKevList, hasApprovedException), a `RiskAcceptance` with an expiry, a `SecurityGatePolicy` that decides block-versus-pass per finding and assigns an SLA, and a `BuildGateEvaluator` that runs all findings and produces a final build verdict. We will run four findings matching the four problems and show the logged decisions and the final pass/fail.
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
security-gate-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/security/
│   │   │   ├── SecurityGateApplication.java        (main class)
│   │   │   ├── model/
│   │   │   │   ├── Severity.java                    (enum)
│   │   │   │   ├── Finding.java
│   │   │   │   └── RiskAcceptance.java
│   │   │   ├── policy/
│   │   │   │   └── SecurityGatePolicy.java
│   │   │   └── gate/
│   │   │       └── BuildGateEvaluator.java
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── security-gate.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/security/
│           └── policy/
│               └── SecurityGatePolicyTest.java
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# security-gate.yml — the machine-readable gate policy
gate:
  block:
    - reachable-critical        # any reachable CRITICAL fails the build
    - kev-listed                # anything on CISA KEV fails regardless of CVSS
    - new-high                  # newly introduced HIGH fails the build
  slas:                         # remediation deadlines in hours
    CRITICAL: 72
    HIGH: 720                   # 30 days
    MEDIUM: 2160                # 90 days
    LOW: 4320                   # 180 days
  exceptions:
    require-approver: true      # developer cannot approve own exception
    max-duration-days: 90       # no exception lasts longer than 90 days
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the gate evaluation demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.security.SecurityGateApplication

# In a real CI step the exit code gates the pipeline:
# java -cp target/classes com.bank.security.SecurityGateApplication || exit 1
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four findings from the scanner — a reachable Critical in fast-json, a non-reachable High in slow-logger, a Critical in legacy-xml that carries a signed exception valid until 2026-12-31, and a Medium in img-codec that is on the CISA KEV list. Today is 2026-10-25.

Step 1: The evaluator receives the list of four findings and loops over them, asking the policy for a verdict on each. Nothing has changed in the data yet; each finding still carries its original signals.

Step 2: For the fast-json Critical, the policy first checks for an exception — there is none. It then checks KEV — false. It then checks "reachable Critical" — true. The policy returns block, logs a SEVERE message, and the evaluator increments its blocker count to 1.

Step 3: For the slow-logger High, there is no exception and it is not on KEV. It is High but it is not reachable and not newly introduced, so none of the block rules fire. The policy returns track-only with a 720-hour SLA and logs an INFO message. The blocker count stays at 1.

Step 4: For the legacy-xml Critical, the policy checks the exception first. The exception is valid on 2026-10-25 because that date is not after the 2026-12-31 expiry. The policy returns do-not-block, logs that the exception is honored with the approver and expiry, and the blocker count stays at 1.

Step 5: For the img-codec Medium, there is no exception. The very first rule, KEV membership, is true, so even though the CVSS severity is only Medium the policy returns block and logs SEVERE. The blocker count rises to 2.

Step 6: The evaluator finishes the loop with a blocker count of 2. Because the count is greater than zero it logs "BUILD FAILED" and returns false. The application prints the final verdict FAIL. The pipeline would translate that false into a non-zero exit code and stop the release.

Final output:

```
INFO: === National Bank of India — payments pipeline security gate ===
SEVERE: BLOCK CVE-2024-1111 — reachable CRITICAL in fast-json
INFO: TRACK CVE-2024-2222 — SLA 720h (no block)
INFO: EXCEPTION honored for CVE-2024-3333 approvedBy=priya.security-lead until=2026-12-31
SEVERE: BLOCK CVE-2024-4444 — on CISA KEV (actively exploited)
SEVERE: BUILD FAILED — 2 blocking finding(s)
INFO: FINAL VERDICT: FAIL
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Scanner output: 4 findings
    │
    ▼
  BuildGateEvaluator.evaluate(findings, today=2026-10-25)
    │  loops each finding → SecurityGatePolicy.shouldBlock()
    │
    ├─ CVE-2024-1111 fast-json CRITICAL reachable
    │     exception? no → KEV? no → reachable CRITICAL? YES
    │     ▼ BLOCK (blockers=1)
    │
    ├─ CVE-2024-2222 slow-logger HIGH not-reachable
    │     exception? no → KEV? no → reachable CRIT? no → new HIGH? no
    │     ▼ TRACK, SLA 720h (blockers=1)
    │
    ├─ CVE-2024-3333 legacy-xml CRITICAL + exception(until 2026-12-31)
    │     exception valid on 2026-10-25? YES
    │     ▼ HONOR EXCEPTION, no block (blockers=1)
    │
    └─ CVE-2024-4444 img-codec MEDIUM onKev=true
          exception? no → KEV? YES
          ▼ BLOCK (blockers=2)
    │
    ▼
  blockers=2 > 0
    ▼
  BUILD FAILED → pipeline exit code 1 → release stopped
```

  [EVALUATED] ──rule hits──→ [BLOCKING] → build fails

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, a failing security scan should be able to block the build, but the engineering skill is in choosing exactly what to block on, because if you block on every High and Critical you flood developers with noise, they lose trust in the gate, and they start bypassing it, which is worse than having no gate at all. So I block on a combination of signals rather than raw severity. I fail the build on any Critical that is actually reachable from our code, on anything that appears on the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list regardless of its CVSS score because that means attackers are using it right now, and on any newly introduced High, because the gate's job is to stop new risk from entering. Pre-existing Mediums and Lows and non-reachable findings do not break the build; they become tracked tickets.

For everything that does not block, I assign remediation SLAs by severity — typically Critical within about seventy-two hours, High within thirty days, Medium within ninety, and Low within a hundred and eighty or formally risk-accepted. The clock starts when the finding is first detected, and I treat mean-time-to-remediate as a program-health metric so the backlog actually shrinks over time rather than just the new issues being caught.

The exception process is what keeps the gate both safe and practical. Sometimes there is genuinely no patch yet, or the fix is a breaking upgrade, or the vulnerable path is provably not exploitable in our configuration. In those cases I allow a risk acceptance, but never as a silent ignore flag buried in a config file. It must record who requested it, a security owner who approved it who is not the developer themselves, the business justification and compensating control, and above all an expiry date, so that when it expires the gate automatically re-blocks and forces a fresh review.

That expiry and approval trail is exactly what makes it auditable — a regulator can ask us to show every risk we have accepted and who signed off, and we can produce that list instantly. At National Bank of India I built precisely this policy engine for our payments pipeline: it honored a signed exception on an unpatched library, tracked a non-reachable High against its SLA, but hard-failed the build on a reachable Critical in our JSON parser and on a medium-severity issue that had landed on the KEV list. The result was a gate engineers actually trusted, because it only stopped them when stopping them was genuinely warranted.
